turns.t: Good morning, Mr. Venkataraman. I have the letter from the urgent care centre in front of me, dated last week. It says you went in after an insect bite became infected, and that there was a problem with the tablets they gave you.

Yes, yes, that is why I came today. The tablets, they gave me for five days. I took the first one on Tuesday... no, no, Thursday, sorry, it was Thursday, and by the evening I was having the hives all over my back.
The hives, so itchy raised patches?
Very itchy. Like I was lying on a bed of ants. My wife counted them and gave up after thirty.
Thirty is a polite place to stop counting. Goodness.
Which tablets were they, do you remember the name? The letter just says antibiotic.
Wait, wait, let me think. It started with A. Amoxyclav, no... Amoxil... the doctor there said it was amoxicillin. Yes. Amoxicillin. I took a photo of the box, but my phone is in the car.
That's quite all right. Amoxicillin is the one on the letter too, so we agree. And did you stop the tablets once the hives began?
I stopped straight away. The nurse told me to, on the phone. And it settled by the weekend.
Good. And you came in on your own today, no one with you?
My wife wanted to come, but she has her yoga on Mondays and she will not miss it for anything.
Good for her. Let me explain how I'd like to handle this, but first, one practical thing. Is there anything you are taking regularly?
Only one tablet. Amlodipine, 5 mg, once daily in the morning. Wait, is it 5 or 10? No, 5. I am sure it is 5, I keep the strip in my wallet.
Five is what I have on file as well, so your wallet and my computer agree.
A rare moment of agreement, I think.
Quite. Anyway, let me do your readings. Blood pressure and temperature first.
Blood pressure is 130 over 80, and the temperature is 37.0, so quite normal.
Good, good, thank you. I was worried it would be high because of the stress of all this.

It's fine. Now, the practical question is what to do with this information. A reaction like hives within hours of a penicillin-type antibiotic should be taken seriously, so I will record it in your notes as an allergy.
Will it be on the computer everywhere? Like if I go to a different hospital?

Within the shared hospital records it usually travels, but the safest thing is that you also tell any doctor or pharmacist yourself. I'd suggest writing it in your phone and your wallet, next to the amlodipine strip.
My daughter will set it up in the phone, she is very good at this sort of thing.

Excellent. There's also a more interesting question, which is whether you are truly allergic or whether the hives came from something else that week. I would like to arrange an allergy skin test, to find out for sure.
A skin test? They put the medicine on the arm?
A tiny amount, with a small scratch or a very fine needle. The specialist team does it in a hospital clinic, so that any reaction is managed safely.
All right.
And until then, can I take anything for fever or pain if it comes?
The usual simple painkillers are fine. The only ones to avoid for now are penicillin-type antibiotics, until the test says otherwise.
Understood. Amoxicillin, amoxyclav, anything with that family. I will tell the pharmacist also.
And do take the photo of the box when you find your phone, it is a good back-up.
It is still in the car. I will bring it up next time I come, or send my daughter.
That's exactly right. The clinic will contact you with a date for the test.
Thank you, doctor. You have cleared my mind. I was thinking all week that I did something wrong.
You did nothing wrong, you did precisely the right thing by stopping them straight away.
Then I will go and tell my wife she can stop counting the hives.
Please do. Good day, Mr. Venkataraman.

chief_complaint.value: that is why I came today

clinical_actions.description: Tell doctors and pharmacists about the reaction and avoid penicillin-type antibiotics until tested
